rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because everyone receives from God alone, asking anyone else ultimately amounts to asking God; others cannot grant or remove anything.
rows.anchor: since everyone who asks receives from God alone, hence irrespective of whom he asks, he in reality asks God for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word may also mean needs: all beings in heaven and earth are needy and depend on God.
rows.anchor: all those in the heavens and the earth are needy and dependent on God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has not delegated the world's administration to alleged deities; He controls the sun and moon, meets human needs, and remains active in every affair, leaving no need for an intercessor.
rows.anchor: God Himself is running all the affairs of this world. He alone controls the movements of the sun and the moon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here yawm means time, a Qur'anic usage; the verse's implication is that people should ask God for whatever they want.
rows.anchor: here means “time” and it is used in this meaning at many places in the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain underscores that God continuously manages the world and that His majesty is visible throughout creation.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has not isolated Himself from the affairs of this world; He is continuously involved in managing and controlling them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-thaqalan denotes both jinn and humankind; its sense of collective weight intensifies the challenge addressed to them together.
rows.anchor: refers to both jinnkind and mankind. Since in their collective capacity both become heavy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the world's term ends, God will turn fully to human accountability, judge every person, and reward or punish; this is creation's real purpose.
rows.anchor: At that time, the Almighty will be free from running this world and direct all His attention to man’s accountability.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section portrays the warned-of Day, and its discourse follows coherently from the preceding warning.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, the Day which people are being warned of is portrayed. The coherence and sequence in the discourse is obvious.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated question means that deniers have rejected the world's clear signs of accountability and asks what they will say when they witness judgement.
rows.anchor: what will they do when they will see the Day of Judgement and the court of God with their very eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming unaccountable power are challenged to escape the boundaries of heaven and earth, which would prove whether they are beyond God's control.
rows.anchor: If they think that they are accountable before no one and have absolute authority, they should just attempt to cross the boundaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sultan here means permission rather than authority: escape requires God's permission, which only God can grant.
rows.anchor: Here it is used in the second of these meanings. However much as they may want to cross the boundaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain asks what signs of divine majesty they will deny if they cannot recognize even their helplessness before God.
rows.anchor: if they are not being able to comprehend even this sign of being helpless and powerless before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat concerns anyone who exceeds God's limits: fire and molten brass will bombard them so profusely that they cannot escape.
rows.anchor: he shall be pelted with flames of fire and molten brass, and such shall be the profuse nature of this bombardment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fiery shuwaz refers to shooting stars hurled at jinn who try to enter the higher heavens and eavesdrop; the jinn admit they cannot escape God's grasp.
rows.anchor: shooting stars about which the Qur’ān has specified that they are pelted at the devils among the jinn

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally take nuhas to mean smoke.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have generally regarded the word

rows.speaker: lexicographers
rows.claim: Some lexicographers give smoke as a rare meaning of nuhas and cite a couplet attributed to the poet Nabighah Dhubyani as evidence.
rows.anchor: Some lexicographers have mentioned it as its rare meaning and have also corroborated this meaning by a couplet of the poet N ābighah Dhubyānī.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The smoke reading is doubtful because the couplet's provenance is disputed and the Qur'an would otherwise replace its own common word for smoke with an unusual one.
rows.anchor: For this reason, I have my reservations in accepting this meaning of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuhas keeps its conventional sense and denotes the metallic material of a shooting star, not smoke.
rows.anchor: is used in its conventional meaning and it is a type of shooting star mentioned by the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meteors heat and dissolve in the atmosphere; surviving meteorites include iron, stone, bronze, and brass components, supporting the verse's reference to brass.
rows.anchor: Just as ingredients of iron and stone have been found in these meteors, similarly ingredients of bronze and brass are also found in it.

rows.speaker: interpreters
rows.claim: Some interpret the sky's comparison as the sediment of oil.
rows.anchor: to mean the sediment of oil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers skin as the meaning because redness suits skin; when stripped, skin exposes red flesh, as the sky will appear when split.
rows.anchor: this word is also commonly used for skin. Since in this meaning, the word is more appropriate to be qualified by redness, I have preferred it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The red, split sky depicts the Day of Judgement and confronts current deniers with God's manifest power.
rows.anchor: today they are denying this day; however, the day will come when the sky shall be rent asunder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denied questioning is investigative scrutiny: criminals need no interrogation because their faces disclose their crimes and deserved punishment; limbs and even hairs also testify.
rows.anchor: the questioning which is refuted relates to investigation and scrutiny. At other places, the Qur’ ān has stated the reason why this would not be required

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questions of rebuke, reprimand, or sarcasm remain possible, so other Qur'anic reports of questioning criminals do not contradict this verse.
rows.anchor: the questions which relate to rebuke, reprimand and sarcasm are concerned, they are not negated here. The questions which are mentioned in the Qur’ ān regarding the criminals are of this second type.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seizing criminals by forelocks and feet depicts their being thrown into Hell like logs; the action is implied by the image rather than stated.
rows.anchor: just as logs of wood are thrown into raging fire, these people shall be thrown into Hell. Here they being thrown into Hell is not stated in words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word an denotes water at its maximum heat, and the condemned will shuttle between Hell's flames and boiling water.
rows.anchor: refers to water whose heat has reached its ultimate temperature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain's placement after the seizure scene says that this phase is imminent and asks which signs of God the deniers will still reject.
rows.anchor: this phase is soon to come before such people; so which of the signs of their Lord will they deny?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the criminals' fate, the passage contrasts the reward of the God-fearing, completing the picture of both groups with coherent discourse.
rows.anchor: After a mention of the fate of the criminals, the forthcoming verses mention the details of reward which the God-fearing will receive in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 46-61 describe the gardens of the near ones to God; the remaining verses describe those of the companions of the right hand, whose status is compared in the paired Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah.
rows.anchor: verses 46-61 mention the details of the Paradise of the muqarrabīn (the near ones to God) and the subsequent verses mention the details of the Paradise of the aṣḥāb al-yam īn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous are defined by fear of standing before God; this fear alone keeps a person on the right path and restrains criminality.
rows.anchor: the only thing which keeps a person on the right path is this fear of facing his Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two gardens express the completion of God's favour and the comprehensive successes of the Hereafter; the two gardens in 18:32 likewise exemplify a completed favour that led its recipient to ingratitude.
rows.anchor: is a comprehensive expression of all the successes of the Hereafter and two orchards are mentioned as a completion of favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrains answer deniers who dismiss the Hereafter and assume poor Muslims cannot share its rewards, while they themselves expect worldly privilege to continue; the gardens are specified for the pious.
rows.anchor: each and every favour of Paradise is singled out and it is stressed that they are specifically for the pious people of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two gardens are densely lush, with abundant branches; this imagery draws on Arabs' pride in orchards and their delight in greenery in a hot, dry land.
rows.anchor: The reason is that the Arabs relished orchards the most and took pride in owning them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fountain in each garden guarantees its luxuriance, prompting the refrain about God's favours.
rows.anchor: As a guarantee for the luxuriance of these orchards, each will have a fountain running in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two gardens offer distinct kinds of fruit; zawj is used in a specific sense explained elsewhere in the work.
rows.anchor: Both orchards will not have the same types of fruit. Each will have its own unique repertoire of fruits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The couches are lined with thick brocade, and fruit hangs close enough to reach without effort.
rows.anchor: the cloth will be lined with thick brocade. In other words, who can imagine the outer lining of cloths which are internally lined with brocade?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fihinna covers all previously mentioned and implicitly understood blessings, including gardens, orchards, and palaces; such pronoun use is common in Arabic.
rows.anchor: is all the favours mentioned earlier as well as all the gardens, orchards and castles of Paradise which may not have been mentioned in words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The maidens are bashful and modest; the author treats bashfulness as beauty and a safeguard of morality, arguing that faithfulness enables a woman to contribute to family life.
rows.anchor: Bashfulness is not only the greatest beauty of a woman, it is also the greatest guard of her morality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The untouched maidens are described as chaste; comparison with rubies and corals conveys both beauty and chastity.
rows.anchor: The comparison with rubies and corals is to bring out their beauty and chastity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ihsan means both virtue and its reward; the verse rhetorically states that virtuous action should receive a virtuous recompense.
rows.anchor: is used for piety as well as for the reward of piety. In this verse, it is used very eloquently in both these meanings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without judgement, God would seem to leave vice and virtue undistinguished and even favor wickedness; human nature instead bears witness to divine justice and mercy, which punish sinners and reward the pious.
rows.anchor: His nature bears witness that the Lord of this universe is very just and merciful. He will punish those who commit sins and greatly reward the pious for their virtues.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The latter two gardens probably belong to the companions of the right hand, while the first two belong to the foremost or near ones; their gardens differ in status.
rows.anchor: what is more probable is that in this sūrah too, the earlier two orchards are meant for the al-sābiqūn or the muqarrabīn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dunihima may mean besides, in contrast with, or lesser than the first two gardens; the refrain signals that further gardens and favours remain.
rows.anchor: can be translated as “besides these two” and “in contrast with these two” as well as “lesser than these two.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gardens' green is so luxuriant that it appears nearly black, the most beautiful color for a lush orchard.
rows.anchor: Such will be the state of greenness of these orchard s that they will appear to be blackish.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word describes forceful, steaming mountain springs, unlike the earlier word for springs that simply flow on level ground.
rows.anchor: used earlier which means that they only flow; however, mountainous springs flow with force and vigour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dates and pomegranates are specified after the general mention of fruit because they are cherished Arabian fruits; the wording differs from the earlier gardens, where each has distinct fruits.
rows.anchor: is a mention of the specific after the general. Both these are cherished fruits of Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The maidens are described as beautiful and pious; tent-dwelling is an especially cherished Arabian image, since affluent tents could surpass palaces in elegance.
rows.anchor: Living in tents was something very cherished in Arabia. The tents of the affluent people of Arabia were even more classy than their castles and palaces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The latter gardens' tent-dwelling maidens differ in qualities from the bashful houris of the first gardens, compared with rubies and corals.
rows.anchor: The readers should keep in mind the difference in qualities of the maidens in both sets of the two orchards.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people recline on green sheets and fine carpets; although the word can describe various rare, costly things, context makes it qualify the carpets.
rows.anchor: is used for rare and expensive things and it can refer to various things keeping in view the context and occasion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing blessing repeats after the reward passage because the Lord's majesty guarantees these favours; God's name signifies His being, as face did earlier.
rows.anchor: The name signifies the entity it stands for.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first gardens evoke tastes more familiar to non-Arabs and the later ones Arabian tastes; the descriptions offer a broad comparison, while their true form is known only to God.
rows.anchor: the favours pointed out in the orchards mentioned earlier reflect more the taste of the non-Arabs, while those mentioned later reflect more the taste of the Arabs.
